Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

dragonfarm 0.4.0

The headline of this release is a document route: drop in PDFs, Word files, web pages, or spreadsheets, ask questions with cited sources, have a model write training questions from them, review those, and fine-tune. The app now opens on it, has a new look with a dark mode, and can train a 7B model in 4-bit on an 8 GB GPU. Everything below was measured on an 8 GB laptop GPU (RTX 4060) and on real documents: R’s own manuals, a 76-page annual report as PDF and as Word, live web pages, and a spreadsheet.

Documents

  • Numbered headings in PDFs (“6.4 Updating packages”) start their section even when the line before them was a long one that ended a sentence; they used to be glued on to the end of the previous paragraph, so the section was never started and search could not find it (26 such headings in R’s installation and data manuals, 29 in An Introduction to R). With R’s two installation and data manuals as a held-out test, the answer reached the top four excerpts for 19 of 20 questions (from 17) and a 7B answered 18 (from 16); on R’s introduction and FAQ, 32 of 32 (from 31).

  • PDF lists printed one entry per line, such as an annual report’s “CALIFORNIA – 140” location counts, keep their entries apart (“;”) instead of running together, and no-break spaces become plain spaces. Asked for eight places’ counts, a 7B read 7 right against 4 with the run-on text; the report’s California count, missed before, is now answered (21 of 23 known-answer questions, from 20).

  • New: dragon_documents() reads PDF, HTML, Markdown, text, Word, spreadsheet files, directories of them, and web pages into a document set: chunks of about 170 words that never cross a heading, each keeping its file, section, and (for PDFs) page, stored under runs_dir/documents/<name>/. Reading again re-reads only files whose contents changed, and a set built by an older version of the readers is re-read rather than reused. dragon_chunks() (with a page column), dragon_documents_load(), and dragon_documents_list() go with it. The Python environment gains pypdf (with cryptography, for encrypted PDFs), python-docx, and openpyxl.

  • dragon_example_documents(): three short policy documents for the fictional company behind the example tickets, so the route can be tried before bringing your own files.

  • PDFs. Pages whose text comes out of the standard extractor as two-letter fragments (Co st co Wh ol es al e, common in annual reports) are re-read in a layout-aware mode: a 76-page annual report went from 726 unreadable chunks to 273 readable ones under real section names. Running headers, page numbers, contents entries with dot leaders, and dot leaders inside table rows are dropped; a sentence broken across pages is rejoined; code, lead-in lines, rows of numbers, and single words are no longer taken for headings (R-intro went from 97 section names, one 1,489 characters long, to 79 real ones); apostrophes a font did not map are restored. A PDF with no text layer (a scan) is reported by name with advice to run OCR first, instead of silently adding nothing.

  • Year columns. In a financial table the years are printed once, above the figures; flattened into text, nothing said which figure was which year, and answers came from the wrong column. Rows under a year header that end in one figure per year now carry the years: “Net cash used in investing activities (2024: (4,409); 2023: (4,972); 2022: (3,915))”. On ten questions about an annual report that need a specific year’s figure, correct answers went from 5 to 9, and confident wrong-column answers from 2 to none. Word tables get the same treatment from a header row of dates, and their merged cells are no longer repeated once per column they span (“249,625 | 249,625”); the Word copy of the report went from 8 to 10 of 10.

  • Units. A note such as “(dollars in millions, except per share data)” is carried into later chunks that show money without a unit word, so answers from financial tables say “$4,409 million” rather than “$4,409”.

  • Word. Unit notes styled as headings set the unit instead of becoming a section; short paragraphs set entirely in bold or italic become headings when prose follows them (the sub-headings of a 10-K are italic), while table column labels, which look the same, stay text. The Word annual report went from one 38-chunk “Note 1” to 123 real sections.

  • Web pages. Blocks made mostly of links and regions marked as navigation, banner, footer, or search are dropped, so a page without a <nav> tag no longer leaks its menu into the first chunk. Heading anchor glyphs (the pilcrow after every R FAQ heading) are removed.

  • Spreadsheets. Each row becomes “column: value” pairs; a two-column label-and-value sheet is read as such rather than as a header plus data; a first row of numbers is not taken for column names; and each sheet starts its own chunk.

  • A manual or FAQ with numbered sections (“2.1 What is R?”) is no longer mistaken for a changelog; changelog-like files are still flagged and down-weighted, and quoted material and code blocks are marked on each chunk.

  • PDFs with outline headings (“I. INTRODUCTION”, “A. General Considerations”, “III. ESTIMANDS (A.3)”), as in FDA and ICH guidances, now get their real sections, and a street address on a cover page is never taken for a heading. Before, the agency’s mailing address labelled 48 of 153 chunks of four FDA guidances. Top-1 retrieval on 18 questions about them rose from 44% to 67% (dense search) and from 61% to 72% (hybrid). Other PDFs read exactly as before. Document sets are re-read on next use (reader version 19).

  • A short PDF (a one-line notice) is read instead of being called scanned; only a PDF with no text at all, or a few words over pictures of pages, is reported as scanned. When every file is a scan, dragon_documents() says so and suggests OCR, instead of listing the supported formats.

  • Reading a folder now says which files it skipped because no reader handles them, in one line grouped by type, with what to save them as (“Skipped 2 files dragonfarm can’t read: 1 .doc (save it as .docx), 1 .pptx (export it to PDF).”). Before, they were left out silently.

  • Encrypted PDFs that open without a password (common for official documents) are read; before, AES-encrypted ones failed with “cryptography is required”. A PDF that needs a password says so in plain words. Text, CSV, and HTML files saved in Windows-1252 or UTF-16 read cleanly instead of with replacement marks for every accented letter. Files in .doc, .xls, .pptx and similar formats are refused with what to save them as. Saved sets read identically (reader version 19).

Asking documents

  • Answers stream as they are written: dragon_ask(on_token = ) and the Ask step in the app show the first words while the rest is still coming. With full answers from a 7B (often 150 words or more), the first words arrived after a median 0.8 seconds against 14 seconds for the whole answer.

  • dragon_chat() and the app’s Try it and Chat steps now allow 600 new tokens by default (was 256 and 200), as dragon_ask() does: with full answers, 21 of 100 benchmark answers from the 7B ran past 150 words and were cut off mid-sentence at the old limits. It is a ceiling, so short answers are no slower.

  • dragon_ellmer_tools() hands dragonfarm’s tools to any ellmer chat, or to Claude Desktop and other MCP clients with dragon_mcp_server(): search a document set (or one document in it), answer from it with citations, check an answer’s figures, read documents, build the training set (saved for a person to read before approving training), list sets and runs, check a run. Every call is checked against the tool’s contract, callers named as agents are held to a policy (some calls are refused, some wait for a person), and every call is recorded in a small catalogue kept in the runs folder.

  • Some protection against instructions planted in documents (“ignore your instructions”, “always say 90 days”, “answer in French”). For 7B-class models the excerpts are datamarked: their words are joined with ^ and the model is told marked text is information only. On 24 questions over documents with planted instructions, the 7B followed 10 of them without it and 5 with it, and answered the FDA test questions exactly as before. It made smaller models worse, so it is off for them; options(dragonfarm.datamark = TRUE) or FALSE forces it. Planted instructions can still get through; check the sources. The two test sets ship with the package, so the rate can be measured again for any model and is recorded in the catalogue (rerun on the 7B: 4 of 12 and 1 of 12 steered, as first measured).

  • dragon_check() now says whether agents are on for this machine. Agents need a model of 3B or larger: on 20 tool-use tasks, 3B and 7B models got 17 and 18 right, 0.5B and 1.5B models 13 and 15. On smaller machines everything still works through the fixed workflows. With a model server connected, the server’s model is the one that counts, so a CPU-only laptop with a server can run agents. An agent’s task keeps a checkpoint after every step; if R stops mid-task, it carries on from there without repeating the tool calls it already made. The policy can name a model per agent, and when an agent cannot finish (its model is too small, it runs out of steps, or it fails) the fixed workflow answers instead; Monitor’s “Last 7 days” counts how often that happened.

  • Settings can run a qualification report: checks that the installation matches what is specified (Python packages against the lock, models pinned to exact versions, safetensors only, the catalogue schema) and that the controls work on throwaway data (the record refuses edits, agents stay within the policy, training waits for a person, blocked data stays put, the personal-data patterns). You download a dated report with each check and its evidence; its SHA-256 goes into the record. It is evidence for a validation, not a validation.

  • “Check for personal data” in the Documents step lists email addresses, phone numbers, US social security numbers, card numbers, and labelled dates of birth and patient or record ids found in a set, each with where it was found, by fixed patterns (no model). Every hit is shown for a person to judge: contact lines of organisations are common in public documents. On the documents tested here it flagged only such contact lines and no numbers, versions or dates by mistake.

  • The policy can be changed in the app: Settings has a Policy card for the tools each agent may use, what waits for a person, where data may go, the four-eyes rule for model sign-off, and agent budgets. Each save is a new version with who changed it and why; older versions stay listed. With options(dragonfarm.admin = FALSE) the card is read-only.

  • A team can share one catalogue on Postgres: set DRAGONFARM_CATALOG to a postgresql:// address (or options(dragonfarm.catalog =) to a function that returns a DBI connection) and every runs folder records its events, approvals, policies and model versions there, append-only as on a laptop. Without it, nothing changes: each runs folder keeps its own SQLite file.

  • More of the record-keeping is in the app, not just in R: Monitor has a “Model versions” card (propose a finished, evaluated run as a version of a named model, then approve, reject or retire it with a stated meaning), and “Run it again and compare” on recorded calls and answers in Activity (8 answers a 3B gave on the FDA guidance replayed identically: the same excerpts, prompt and answer; when they differ it says whether the set was re-read, the model changed, or other excerpts were found), and “Download the record (CSV)” for an auditor (the export itself is recorded with a SHA-256 of the file). Activity opens with a “Last 7 days” line: what happened, what was refused or failed, what left the machine and to where, and how many approvals are waiting. The Documents step has “Check it re-reads the same”, which reads a set’s files again and says whether they come back identical.

  • Answers in the Documents step get a quick check that needs no model: every figure in the answer (numbers, dates, percentages, versions) must appear in its excerpts or the question, and every citation must point at an excerpt. A plain line appears only when something is off (“Check this: 4.0 is not in the excerpts.”). On 224 recorded answers from 1.5B and 3B models it flagged one, a real wrong figure, with no false alarms, and it caught 37 of 37 figures changed by hand. It cannot catch a real figure used wrongly, or wrong words: 10 of 11 wrong answers there had no figure to check. ellmer chats and MCP clients get it as the check_answer tool.

  • Chat counts your thumbs up, thumbs down and edits, and “Train on my feedback” turns the liked and edited replies (with the turns before them) into a training set, ready in Train. Before, this needed dragon_feedback() in R.

  • The Data step loads chat-format JSONL (a messages list per row, the format Chat exports) as whole conversations, ready to train without a Map step. Before, multi-turn training needed dragon_conversations().

  • The app passes an automated WCAG 2.1 A/AA check (axe-core 4.10.2) on every tab, in light and dark mode; before, it flagged 68 places under 5 rules. The page declares its language, the hardware badge and dark-mode switch sit outside the tab list, warning and success text are dark enough to read, and every text box and drop-down has a label for screen readers. The check covers the app as it first opens, not every result card.

  • The app has a Settings page for the keys of outside services (Hugging Face, the Claude API, Kaggle, Lightning AI, OpenRouter, Groq): paste a key once, and it is checked and kept in the computer’s own keychain (through the ‘keyring’ package), never in scripts or files. Kaggle’s downloaded kaggle.json is picked up from Downloads with one click. Free tiers are turned on there too, with a daily cap. Messages that used to say “set HF_TOKEN in the R session” now point to Settings.

  • Training on a free cloud GPU from the app takes fewer steps. One button packs the run, saves it to your Downloads folder and opens the notebook, which now asks Colab and Kaggle for a GPU by itself. In Colab you press Run all and pick the file; when the results land in Downloads, the app imports them. The steps the app shows no longer include any code. With a Kaggle key (kaggle.json), Kaggle needs no clicks at all: the app uploads the run as a private dataset, starts the notebook on a GPU, waits, and imports the results, showing where it is as it goes. Lightning AI works the same way with your Lightning keys: the app starts a GPU Studio, trains, brings the results back and stops the Studio, even if something fails.

  • Every answer from documents (dragon_ask(), the Ask step, and chats with documents) is recorded in the runs folder’s catalogue with what it came from: the exact chunks (checksum) and reader, the model and its pinned revision, the settings, every excerpt shown to the model and whether it was cited, and the answer. The answer’s $trace holds the record’s number; the Monitor tab’s Activity card shows it.

  • Everything that sends data off the machine (the Claude API, fetching web pages as documents, publishing to Hugging Face, a model server elsewhere) now passes one check and is recorded in the runs folder’s catalogue with where it went and why. An admin can limit the hosts in the policy, down to none at all.

  • For servers and machines without the internet, the package ships a lock of its Python packages (inst/python/requirements.lock, pinned with hashes, all platforms, from PyPI) and a new article, “Install without the internet”. An environment built from it offline, with an empty cache, was identical to one built online. With DRAGONFARM_PYTHON set, dragon_check() says whether the environment matches the lock.

  • dragon_resume() after a crash is sturdier. A checkpoint cut short by the crash is skipped for the one before it; the run’s log keeps what came before the crash (it used to be replaced); steps trained again are no longer drawn twice in the loss chart; a run that crashed before its first checkpoint starts again instead of failing. GRPO runs now resume with their adapter weights and optimizer state (they used to resume the step count only, from fresh weights). Checked by killing runs mid-way: a resumed 135M fine-tune ended at eval loss 1.188, against 1.189 for the same run without a crash.

  • dragon_ask(compare = TRUE), and “Look for documents that disagree” in the app’s Ask step, help when documents give different versions of the same rule. The usual top excerpts stay; two more are added that are relevant but say something different (a rule repeated by many documents otherwise crowds out the one later document that changed it), and the model is asked to give each document’s version. On a test set of six such rules, both versions reached the model 6 of 6 times instead of 3 or 4, and a 7B named both in 13 of 24 answers instead of 6. It still sometimes calls differing documents consistent, so check the sources. dragon_retrieve(extra = ) exposes the extra excerpts on their own.

  • Chat with documents understands short follow-ups. “And a boxplot?” or “Which ones, then?” names nothing to search for, so such a turn (ten words or fewer, leaning on the last one with “it”, “those”, “what about” and the like) keeps its own best two excerpts and fills the rest from a search with the previous question in front. On 22 follow-ups about the FDA guidances and R’s manuals the right excerpt came back for 19 instead of 16; 12 changes of topic and 57 longer follow-ups were unaffected.

  • Full answers from documents: dragon_ask() and chat with documents ask models of 3B and up for complete answers with the figures, steps, or code the excerpts hold, instead of one short sentence. On 75 questions with known answers the 7B now gets all 75 right (was 72) and the 3B 70 (was 65), still declining all 25 the documents do not cover; answers are longer (a median of 60 words for the 7B) and take about twice as long. Smaller models keep the short instructions, since full answers made them invent more. max_new_tokens now defaults to 600.

  • Untrained models under 3B get one more line in their instructions when answering from documents: “If no excerpt states the answer, reply only: ‘The documents do not cover this.’” Over 55 answerable and 20 unanswerable questions, wrong or made-up answers fell from 33 to 25 (0.5B) and from 21 to 10 (1.5B, the default on CPUs and small GPUs, which now declines all 20 unanswerable questions). The same line made a 3B refuse questions it could answer (8 to 18 bad answers) and did nothing for a 7B, so larger and fine-tuned models do not get it.

  • With four or more excerpts, the keyword search’s best match is always among them, as the embedding’s best already was. A rare exact word (“boxplot”) put its chunk first by keywords but far down by embedding, and the combined ranking dropped it. Questions about R’s manuals with the answer in the top four: 30 to 31 of 32; a 7B answered all 23 known-answer questions on the annual report PDF (from 22). Other sets unchanged.

  • A question that names a year now finds the table row labelled with that year. Rows read as “Net sales (2024: $249,625; 2023: $237,710)” carry a keyword per labelled year, which a question mentioning 2023 searches for; a bare “2023” appears all over a report and did little. Known-answer questions on the annual report reaching the top four excerpts: PDF 85 to 95 percent, Word 85 to 100 percent, other sets unchanged. A 7B answered 22 of 23 on the PDF (from 21) and stayed at 23 of 23 on the Word copy.

  • New: dragon_index() embeds a document set with a small encoder (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, kept warm in the inference worker), dragon_retrieve() returns the most relevant chunks, and dragon_ask() puts them in front of a model as numbered excerpts and returns the answer with its sources, marking which were cited: “report.pdf, p. 68 › Item 14”. The model defaults to the one dragon_check() recommends for the GPU and can be any run, model id, or server backend. dragon_chat() gains documents and k; $sources() shows the excerpts behind the last reply.

  • Retrieval is hybrid by default: the embedding ranking is combined with a keyword (BM25) ranking over each chunk’s section title and text, counting only chunks that share a word with the question, and the embedding’s own best match always stays among the excerpts. Exact terms and figures that a small embedding model ranks a few places too low still reach the answer. The share of questions whose source chunk was among the four excerpts, embedding alone against hybrid: R’s manuals 90.7 to 94.5 percent (616 questions), the package documentation 88 to 100, a spreadsheet 83 to 100; on an annual report the right chunk is ranked first for 75 to 83 percent of questions, up from 58 to 67. dragon_retrieve(method = "dense") keeps the embedding ranking alone, and scripts/retrieval_eval.py measures both on any indexed sets.

  • On the annual report the default 7B in 4-bit answers 20 to 23 of 23 factual questions with known answers (Word copy 23, PDF 20 to 21), including ten that need a specific year’s figure from a table. The PDF misses a total printed inside a map graphic, and the model says so rather than guessing. Six excerpts instead of four did not help.

From documents to training data

  • dragon_questions(mix = TRUE), the new default, asks for a mix of question types per chunk: a “what” or “which”, a “why” or “how”, and, where the passage compares two things, a “how do they differ”. On four FDA guidances comparison questions rose from 11 to 98 of the kept pairs and why/how questions from 113 to 142; 81 percent of pairs were kept instead of 89, and a 3B trained on either set answered the same 23 of 24 test questions. mix = FALSE asks for any three questions, as before.

  • dragon_questions_dataset() adds “not covered” rows by default (negatives = 0.15): a question shown with excerpts from another section, answered “The documents do not cover this.” Without them every training prompt contains its answer and tuned models answer everything. On R’s manuals, a tuned 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B declined 0, 1, and 5 of 15 questions the manuals do not cover; with negatives all three declined 15 of 15, while answerable questions went from 24 to 26, 29 to 28, and 30 to 30 of

    1. Wrong, made-up, or wrongly declined answers over all 47 questions fell from 23 to 6 (0.5B), 17 to 4 (1.5B), and 12 to 2 (3B). (Measured with this release’s reading and search, both sides.)

  • New: dragon_questions() has a model write questions and answers from each chunk (the local model recommended for the machine, in the background, or a teacher such as dragon_llm_anthropic()), runs deterministic filters, and returns every pair with keep and a reason. With the default 7B, 78 to 87 percent of pairs passed on real documents; a small generator does far worse, so review is part of the workflow. A batch that runs out of GPU memory is retried one chunk at a time, and long passages are capped. dragon_questions_save() records your decisions.

  • dragon_questions_dataset() builds the training set with retrieved excerpts in front of each question, always including the chunk the pair was written from, and appends that excerpt’s number to the answer (cite = TRUE) so a tuned model keeps citing. It warns if the document set was re-read after the questions were written.

The app

  • The app opens from RStudio’s Addins menu (“dragonfarm”), no code needed.

  • Every model choice in the app has an (i) icon: hovering over it, or focusing it with the keyboard, shows how the four model sizes compare on that task, as measured for the “Choosing a model size” article. Answering (“Answered by” in Ask, the run in Chat): wrong answers, “not covered” replies, and speed. Writing questions (“Written by” in Teach): pairs kept and how many were correct. Training (the Model step and Try it): results after fine-tuning, training time, and GPU memory.

  • The app starts with documents. A new Documents tab is tab 1: drop files or add web pages, read and index, ask with sources, continue in Chat. Its Teach card generates questions in the background, shows the yield as it grows, and lets you tick and untick pairs grouped by chunk before Continue to Model, which skips Data and Map. The table route (Data and Map first) is one link away or dragon_app(route = "table").

  • Panels take their natural height and the page scrolls; the Map step’s drop slots and the Try it cards are no longer clipped. A message now says to wait for “Upload complete” when Read and index is pressed while a large file is still uploading.

  • A new look that matches dragonfarm.dev: a dark navbar whose tabs read as numbered steps, a one-line introduction on each step, the website’s fonts and amber-to-coral accents, model presets as selectable cards with size, memory, and licence, a loss chart in the same colours, and a dark mode switch in the navbar.

  • The Training step can load the model in 4-bit (QLoRA), so a 7B trains from the app on an 8 GB NVIDIA card. The box ticks itself, with gradient checkpointing, when the chosen model’s full-precision weights would crowd the GPU (a 3B or 7B on 8 GB), sets batch size 1 with gradient accumulation raised to keep the effective batch, and says so when there is no NVIDIA GPU.

Hardware and models

  • dragon_presets() adds Qwen 2.5 3B and 7B, both trained in 4-bit (a 3B peaks at 4.3 GB on 1,536-token document prompts, a 7B at 7.9 GB), and its notes now say which task each size suits. A new load_in_4bit column says which presets need 4-bit to fit. On the documents route the app’s Model step starts from the model the hardware check recommends (a 7B at 8 GB, a 3B at 6 GB) and warns when a model under 3B is chosen for documents. The measurements behind this are in a new article, “Choosing a model size”.

  • Training computes its loss through the output layer in chunks, so the scores for the whole vocabulary are never held at every position at once. With a 151,000-token vocabulary that tensor was about a gigabyte per row at 1,536 tokens. Training a 0.5B on 616 document pairs at 1,536 tokens ran out of memory on an 8 GB card; it now peaks at 6.2 GB and takes 8 minutes, where turning on gradient checkpointing to make it fit took 29. The loss and its gradients are identical to the model’s own (tested). It is used only for batches whose full scores would exceed 256 MB (DRAGONFARM_CHUNKED_LOSS_MB); shorter batches keep the original path, which kept a 7B in 4-bit on short rows at 13 seconds a step where always chunking took 54. DRAGONFARM_FULL_LOSS turns it off entirely. With it, a 7B in 4-bit trains on 1,536-token document prompts on an 8 GB card (616 pairs, three epochs, 4.3 hours); the tuned 7B matched the untrained one on accuracy and always cited its excerpt.

  • 4-bit loading for generation, on Windows as well as Linux. dragon_backend_local(load_in_4bit = "auto") quantizes a model to NF4 only when its full weights would not fit the GPU, so a 7B runs on an 8 GB card (about 5.5 GB of weights) while a 3B still loads in full precision. dragon_check() reports whether 4-bit loading is available and which model it would use: a 1.5B under 6 GB, a 3B at 6 to 8 GB, a 7B in 4-bit at 8 GB and up. QLoRA training (dragon_hardware(load_in_4bit = TRUE)) works on Windows: three epochs of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the 190 example tickets took 22 minutes on the 8 GB card, peaked at 7.9 GB, and reproduced the example policies on held-out tickets where the 0.5B had drifted.

  • dragon_check() reports GPU memory already held by other programs and lists dragonfarm processes started by other R sessions; training warns about them, and dragon_worker_stop(all = TRUE) stops them.

  • Generating for several prompts at once runs them in batches of eight: eight short prompts through a 0.5B went from 17 to 37 seconds to 6.

Name and look

  • A dragon of its own: a new hex logo, favicon, and app icon with an original dragon, the slogan “Raise your own dragon”, and a lighter voice in the app’s step headings and on the website. Model cards in the app show a life stage (Egg, Hatchling, Drake, Wyvern, Elder) beside the size. Function names and error messages are unchanged.

  • Replies in the app are shown as formatted text: lists, bold, and code blocks render instead of raw Markdown. Nothing a model writes can add its own markup: raw HTML is escaped, links other than http(s) and mailto are neutralised, and images are dropped.

  • The GitHub repository is now tejas4patel/dragonfarm, matching the package name: pak::pak("tejas4patel/dragonfarm"). Old tejas4patel/dragon-farm links keep working through GitHub’s redirect.

Fixes

  • Training, writing practice questions, evaluating, and merging now refuse to start while another of them is running on the GPU (in any R session), saying which job is in the way. Two at once on an 8 GB card fail in ways that look like bugs. options(dragonfarm.allow_parallel_gpu = TRUE) turns the check off.

  • Practice questions from models that wrap their labels in Markdown (**Q1:**) are no longer thrown away: a 1.5B wrote every label in bold and none of its 22 pairs were kept; now all 22 parse. Every earlier question set re-parses identically (3,362 pairs).

  • Preset models are pinned to the Hub commit they were tested with, and runs record it, so a run trains and answers with exactly those weights even if the model’s page changes later. Models load from safetensors only: weights that exist only in the older pickle (.bin) format can run code when loaded and are refused with a plain message, unless you set options(dragonfarm.allow_pickle_weights = TRUE) for a model you trust.

  • A model id with a typo (“Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruc”) now says there is no such model and suggests the closest preset, instead of passing on a message about private repositories and tokens.

  • The Monitor shows “Cancel run” only while a run is queued or running, and “Resume from checkpoint” only after it failed or was cancelled; both used to show for every run, finished ones included.

  • dragon_ask() asks once more, in the same conversation, when a model replies with nothing but a citation marker such as “[1]”. The 3B did this on 6 of 65 benchmark questions; with the retry it left none empty and answered 28 of 32 questions about R’s manuals instead of 24. Chat with documents (dragon_chat(documents = ) and the app’s Chat tab) does the same. If the second reply is only a marker too, a third, plain attempt gets just the cited excerpt and the question; on 100 benchmark questions the 1.5B was left with a bare “[2]” twice and now with none (one of the two now right). An answer written in brackets, like “[R_LIBS_USER]”, is no longer mistaken for a citation.

  • The app no longer slows to a crawl with many runs. Seven panels each listed every file under the runs folder every three seconds, checkpoints and indexes included; with a thousand files that took about a second a time and kept the app busy. They now look two levels deep (7.5 times faster here). The Monitor also stopped resetting a run you had just picked back to the newest one when the run list refreshed.

  • A training run that runs out of GPU memory now says so, with the usual fixes, including when the error arrives as CUBLAS_STATUS_EXECUTION_FAILED (a 7B in 4-bit at batch size 4 on an 8 GB card) rather than “out of memory”.

  • A background pipeline that was cancelled or stopped left an Rscript* file in the temporary folder on Windows, because the code was passed with Rscript -e. Pipelines now run from a script file next to their record.

  • After the local model stopped answering in time (or a request was interrupted), its late reply was taken as the answer to the next question, so every later answer was one question behind. Requests to the inference worker now carry an id and replies to another request are skipped; a worker that times out is stopped and the next call starts a fresh one.

  • dragon_questions() no longer errors at the very end of a long run. The generator reports every chunk done a moment before it writes “done”; the progress bar closed itself at 100 percent and the next update failed with “Cannot find progress bar”, after all the questions had been written.

  • A run is no longer marked failed by an out-of-memory error in the evaluation after training. Held-out loss is computed in chunks through the output layer, optimizer state is released first, and a run whose evaluation still cannot fit succeeds with an eval_warning. Peak evaluation memory at 4 x 1536 tokens fell from 7.9 GB to 2.4 GB with the same loss. dragon_train_args() gains eval_batch_size (default 1).

  • Large requests to the inference worker no longer hang: replies longer than processx’s line buffer are reassembled, and big requests are written in a loop.

  • dragon_example_data() no longer contains duplicate tickets, so held-out numbers are not inflated by verbatim repeats. The tickets are synthetic; treat them as a smoke test, not a benchmark.

dragonfarm 0.3.4

CRAN release: 2026-10-12

  • Fixed a test that failed on macOS (CRAN’s M1mac additional check) though it passed everywhere else. It compared dragon_runs_dir()’s default, a directory that does not exist yet, against tempdir() after normalizePath(); on macOS that resolves /var to /private/var for the existing tempdir() but leaves the nonexistent path unresolved, so the prefix check failed. The test now compares the existing parent directory. No change to package code or behaviour.

dragonfarm 0.3.3

CRAN release: 2026-10-07

  • Fixed the Shiny app’s Try it, Chat, Train, and Pipeline panels sometimes keeping a stale runs list until the page was reloaded – most visibly, a run that had just finished training would not appear as selectable in Try it. Their reactivePoll()s watched only each run’s own status.json mtime, which misses a change when the file that actually matters (the adapter, or a run’s directory being renamed by archive/restore) is written or moved without status.json itself changing again. All of the app’s run-list pollers now share runs_change_signature(), which changes whenever any file anywhere under the runs directory is added, edited, or moved.

dragonfarm 0.3.2

  • The 0.3.1 fix for the torchao ImportError on cloud GPUs (pinning torchao>=0.16.0 in requirements) turned out not to be reliably honoured on Colab’s and Kaggle’s preinstalled environment (pip reported success but the old 0.10.0 build was still what got imported). The requirements pin is reverted, and the shared remote notebook (inst/remote/dragonfarm_remote.ipynb, used by dragon_remote() for Colab, Kaggle, Lightning AI, and RunPod) now explicitly uninstalls torchao after installing the trainer’s requirements. dragonfarm never imports torchao itself, and peft’s LoRA dispatch skips its torchao check cleanly when the package is entirely absent rather than present at an old version, so removing it sidesteps the problem instead of depending on pip to upgrade it in place.

dragonfarm 0.3.1

  • Fixed cloud training (dragon_remote() on Colab, Kaggle, Lightning AI, and RunPod) failing with ImportError: Found an incompatible version of torchao. dragonfarm never uses torchao, but recent peft versions probe it while dispatching LoRA and raise instead of skipping when an older version is already installed, which Colab and Kaggle’s base images ship by default. dragon_python_requirements() now pins torchao>=0.16.0 so the bundled requirements.txt installs a compatible version.

dragonfarm 0.3.0

CRAN maintainers reviewed 0.1.1 and asked for several changes, folded into this release along with everything added since 0.2.0:

  • Where runs are stored by default has changed. dragon_runs_dir() used to default to dragonfarm_runs under the working directory; a package must not write there without being asked. It now defaults to dragonfarm_runs under a session temp directory, so a fresh R session never writes to your project or home folder on its own, and that folder disappears when the session ends. For runs you want to keep, set options(dragonfarm.runs_dir = "path/to/dragonfarm_runs") or the DRAGONFARM_RUNS_DIR environment variable once, or pass runs_dir= to the function you’re calling. See ?dragon_runs_dir and the README.
  • Fixed three places (dragon_judge(), dragon_split(), dragon_synthesize()/dragon_prompts()) that saved and restored .Random.seed by hand for a seeded sample; they now use withr::with_seed(), which does the same thing without dragonfarm’s own code touching .GlobalEnv. withr moved from Suggests to Imports. dragon_resume()’s log line now goes through a small file-append helper rather than cat().
  • Examples that need Python, a GPU, or a model download now use if (interactive()) instead of \dontrun{}, so R CMD check at least parses them; they still don’t run during checks or on CRAN’s servers.
  • Package and software names in the Title and Description fields are now quoted and cased correctly ('Python', 'shiny'), and quotes were removed from LoRA, which is a technique name, not a package.
  • Added testthat-based tests for the three app modules (Data, Model, Try it) that had none, covering their server logic without needing a real Shiny session, Python, or a GPU.

Everything else added since 0.2.0

  • dragon_reward("command", command = ...): a reward for dragon_reinforce() that runs a command (a test suite, a linter) against the completion and scores by its exit code or a number in its stdout. Runs the command directly, never through a shell, so the completion’s own text cannot inject anything into the command line.

  • The Chat tab streams replies token by token, for the local worker and for server backends alike, instead of showing the whole reply only once generation finishes. Compare mode still shows each side’s full reply once it lands.

  • Starting a training run now stops the local inference worker first, if one is loaded from an earlier Try it or Chat call. Two heavy Python/CUDA processes starting at the same moment has occasionally crashed a fresh trainer on Windows; freeing the worker’s GPU memory first is the most likely trigger and costs nothing, since the worker restarts automatically on the next generation call.

  • The Python side (inst/python) is now also its own installable package: pip install ./inst/python (or a built wheel) gives a dragonfarm command (check, train, generate, pack) and a dragonfarm.api module (Run, runs()) for reading a run directory from plain Python, with no R involved. A run started from R can be inspected or continued from Python and back, since both read and write the same files. Not yet published to PyPI.

  • Runs can be archived, restored, and deleted. dragon_archive_run() moves a run’s directory under archived/ (every file kept; it just drops out of dragon_runs() and the app); dragon_unarchive_run() brings it back; dragon_delete_run() removes it for good. Both refuse a run that is queued or running, or one that another run continues from, unless force = TRUE. The Monitor panel gets Archive and Delete buttons (Delete asks for confirmation first), a “Show archived” toggle, and Restore.

  • Chat gets context limits, a second backend to compare with, and transcript round-tripping in the app. dragon_chat(context_window=) tracks an approximate token budget and automatically drops the oldest turns to stay under it; $context_usage() reports tokens used, the window, and how many turns were dropped. The Chat tab shows a warning banner near the limit, a “Compare with a second backend” toggle sends the same message to a second backend or run side by side (feedback stays scoped to the primary conversation), and Load transcript / Export as training example round out Save transcript.

  • Fixed a bug in the Chat tab (introduced while building the above) where Shiny’s default “suspend when hidden” behaviour left the conversation panes permanently blank the first time the tab was opened, because they sit behind a renderUI() rather than being part of the tab’s static markup; the affected outputs now opt out of that suspension.

  • dragon_synthesize() gets a quality pass and a judge filter. It now drops replies that are too short or too long, look garbled or wrong-script, repeat an earlier prompt, or repeat (or nearly repeat) an earlier response, before writing the dataset. Passing a judge scores every surviving reply and keeps only the ones at or above min_score, for teacher distillation with a quality gate – pass a run’s own prompts (dragon_prompts(run, "train")) to distill and filter in one call.

  • The app no longer freezes on long actions. Evaluate, Run judge, Build preference pairs, and Merge run as one-step background pipelines; the panel shows progress, the result appears when it lands, and the Pipeline panel lists them.

  • dragon_pipeline_cancel() and a Cancel button on running pipelines. A training step in flight stops after saving a checkpoint; other steps finish first. Records now carry the runner’s pid, so a pipeline whose process died reads as failed instead of running forever.

  • dragon_step_merge(): a pipeline step that writes the latest run as a standalone model.

  • dragon_publish(): push a run’s merged model or adapter to a repo on the Hugging Face Hub, creating it if needed. dragon_step_publish() for pipelines, and a Publish card in the app’s Try it panel.

  • Human feedback becomes data. In dragon_chat() and the app’s Chat panel, replies can be rated up or down, edited, or regenerated; every verdict is saved under feedback/. dragon_feedback() turns them into a conversations dataset of liked and edited replies and a preference-pairs dataset where the same prompt drew a liked and a disliked reply.

  • dragon_conversations(): whole multi-turn conversations as training data, from a list, a JSONL file, or a data frame. They train wherever prompt and response rows do.

  • Two new vignettes: the post-training loop, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

  • Inference backends. dragon_generate() and everything built on it now route through a backend: dragon_backend_local() is a Python worker that keeps the last two models loaded, so repeated calls no longer reload the model; dragon_backend_server() talks to any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint (vLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio, hosted services), and dragon_backend_ollama() to Ollama. dragon_serve_ollama() merges a run and registers it with Ollama in one call. dragon_worker_stop() frees the worker’s memory. Set a session default with options(dragonfarm.backend).

  • dragon_chat(): a conversation object with memory, streaming through on_token where the backend supports it, save and load of transcripts, and export of a conversation as a training example. The app gains a Chat panel with a backend selector and a system prompt.

dragonfarm 0.2.0

  • Pipelines. dragon_pipeline() chains stages built from dragon_step_*() constructors (train, synthesize pairs, prefer, reinforce, judge, evaluate), threading each stage’s run into the next and writing a record after every step. background = TRUE runs it in a separate R process; dragon_pipeline_status() follows it. dragon_compare() accepts a pipeline. The app gains a Pipeline panel that launches the standard recipe and shows every run’s lineage.

  • Reinforcement learning. dragon_map_prompts() maps prompts with an optional reference answer, dragon_reward() defines verifiable rewards (exact, contains, numeric, regex, JSON, length, keyword, or a custom Python function), and dragon_reinforce() runs GRPO: the model samples a group of answers per prompt, the rewards score them, and it learns from the ones that beat their group’s average, with a KL penalty towards the model it started from. Implemented in the package’s own trainer, so no new dependency. Evaluation reports mean held-out reward per reward; the app’s Map and Train panels gain an RL mode with a reward builder.

  • Synthetic data closes the loop. dragon_synthesize() has a teacher model answer your prompts to make fine-tuning data; dragon_synthesize_pairs() samples a run’s own replies, has a judge score them, and keeps the best and worst as preference pairs (or pairs a teacher’s reply against the student’s). dragon_prompts() pulls prompts from a run’s data files. dragon_llm_anthropic() and dragon_llm_ellmer() turn the Claude API or any ellmer chat into a teacher; the judge variants are now wrappers over them. The app’s Try it panel gains an Improve card that builds pairs from the selected run and loads them for the next stage.

  • Evaluation that can drive decisions. dragon_evaluate() gains metrics: deterministic task checks (exact match, token F1, JSON validity, numeric answers, length, custom functions) over every held-out row. dragon_judge() scores a run’s replies with a language model or compares them pairwise with the model it started from, with position swapping so a biased judge produces ties rather than wins; dragon_judge_anthropic() talks to the Claude API directly and dragon_judge_ellmer() wraps any ellmer chat, and any local model can judge too. dragon_compare() puts every run’s measurements side by side. The app gains task metrics and a comparison table in Monitor and a Judge card in Try it.

  • Post-training stages. dragon_map_pairs() maps prompt, chosen, and rejected columns, and dragon_prefer() runs preference optimization on them with DPO or ORPO. Any function that takes a model also accepts a finished run: its adapters are folded into the weights before the new stage adds its own, so fine-tune then prefer chains naturally, locally or through the cloud bundle. Runs record their stage, dragon_evaluate() reports preference accuracy and reward margin, and the app’s Map and Train panels gain a preference-pairs mode and a “Start from” run picker.

  • Driver download link updated to NVIDIA’s canonical URL, which CRAN’s URL check had flagged as a redirect.

dragonfarm 0.1.1

  • dragon_check() now explains a CPU-only result on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU: no driver, a driver too old for the installed torch, or a CPU-only torch build, each with the one-line fix.
  • README gains a Requirements section covering the driver requirement, disk space, and that the CUDA Toolkit is not needed.
  • New dragon_bundle(), dragon_remote(), and dragon_import() take a run to a cloud GPU (Google Colab, Kaggle, Lightning AI, or RunPod) and bring the trained adapter back, for machines without a GPU. dragon_remote_providers() lists the providers. The app gains the same path in its Train and Monitor panels, and dragon_check() points to it when it finds no GPU.

dragonfarm 0.1.0

First release.

  • dragon_dataset(), dragon_map(), and dragon_split() turn a table into chat-format training data with glue templates for combining columns.
  • dragon_train() runs LoRA fine-tuning of any Hugging Face causal language model in a background Python process. Runs live on disk and survive the R session; dragon_run() reopens them.
  • dragon_status(), dragon_progress(), dragon_logs(), dragon_wait(), dragon_cancel(), and dragon_resume() manage a run.
  • dragon_evaluate(), dragon_generate(), and dragon_merge() cover held-out evaluation, generation from the adapter or the base model, and merging into a standalone model. dragon_export_gguf() wraps the llama.cpp converter when one is available.
  • dragon_app() launches a Shiny app with drag-and-drop dataset upload, drag-and-drop column mapping, a live loss curve, and a before-and-after comparison panel. dragon_code() returns the R script for any run.
  • Python dependencies are declared with reticulate::py_require() and built automatically. On Windows with an NVIDIA GPU the CUDA build of torch is selected on first use.
